prompt:
A simulated brick world had this hidden rule:
In this world each placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor: a brick dx cells wide chosen at column x lands at column 8 - dx - x, in the same row. The valid-action mask is in the agent's own action terms. The designs and scoring are as described.

Below is what an AI scientist wrote during a search in that world: its analysis at every round, in order, and the
name and hypothesis of the trial it ended with. Does the text, anywhere, state the rule?
- "yes": it states the rule's substance (what is changed and how).
- "partly": it identifies the right kind of change but not its specifics.
- "no": anything else.

## Analysis at each round
### Round 1
The starting network learned to press DONE at once in every episode (episode length 1.0 by 50% of training). Here is why I think it happens. Every placement lands at the left-right mirror of the chosen anchor. The baseline scores each action only from conv features near the anchor, with a 5x5 receptive field, so for most columns it cannot see the cells the brick will actually fill. Placements then look like random noise with negative mean reward, and DONE at 0 reward wins. The fix should be architectural: the scoring head needs features from the mirrored location. With footprint pooling, mirroring the final feature map along x lines each footprint up exactly with the cells it fills. I test three things: a fixed reflection of the features (flips in x and y, offered as extra channels), a learned mixing layer along each axis that can discover the mirror itself, and the reflection with a higher entropy bonus to resist the DONE collapse. Any nonzero score beats the baseline's 0.000, but the task notes that runs can succeed or fail on seed luck, so small differences between these three still need care.

### Round 2
The mirror rule is the main obstacle. A fixed left-right flip of the features before the head (r1c1) took dev success from 0.000 to 0.726; the seed-0 traces show bricks at the correct mirrored cells. Learning the remap with axis-mixing layers (r1c2, 0.045) was too slow for this budget. A larger entropy bonus (r1c3, 0.626) did not help; that gap is within seed noise, since r1c1's own seeds differ by 0.12. r1c1's training success was still rising at the end (0.34 at 75%, 0.67 at 100%), with only about 29 updates of 4096 samples. So the limit is likely samples or updates, not capacity. The remaining errors are small ordering or overhang mistakes. This round makes two one-change recipe edits to r1c1 (fewer PPO epochs for more samples; smaller batches for more updates) and tests one architecture idea: flip once after the first 1x1 layer, so the 3x3 trunk and head work in the agent's own action frame at about the starting compute.

### Round 3
The mirror rule was the main obstacle. Fixed flipped copies of the features (r1c1, 0.726) work much better than a learned axis remap (r1c2, 0.045). Flipping in the trunk (r2c3, 0.756) gives about the same result. After that, the recipe changes helped. Two PPO epochs, which nearly doubles the samples, gave 0.871. Smaller batches, which double the number of updates, gave 0.840. Both beat r1c1 by more than seed noise (about 0.06). Higher entropy did not help. Training success was still rising at the end of every run, and runs take about 60 s of the 900 s limit, so the agent is short of samples and updates, not wall-clock time. Dev IoU is about 0.98 with about 0.5 extra cells per episode, so failures are small mistakes. This round combines the two winning recipe changes, then pushes further to 1 epoch (about 387k samples) and tests a longer horizon (gamma 0.99) to give the exact-build bonus more weight.

### Round 4
Mirroring the features is the key fix. Models with mirrored features score 0.63–0.87, while the starting network and the learned remapping score 0.00–0.04. Under fixed compute, more fresh samples help: going from 4 to 2 PPO epochs raised dev success from 0.726 to 0.871 (r2c1). One epoch collapsed to choosing DONE immediately. Combining 2 epochs with smaller batches was unstable, with one seed at 0.27 (r3c1). With smaller batches, gamma 0.99 brought that combination back to 0.838 with stable seeds (r3c3). Remaining failures are near misses (IoU about 0.98, about 0.5 extra cells per episode), so longer-horizon credit may help. The action-frame trunk (r2c3) was cheaper and slightly better than concatenation at 4 epochs (within noise) but was never tried with the better recipe. Since this is the last round, I prefer changes to the best that should be stable across seeds.

## Trial it ended with
name: Reflection head, 2 PPO epochs
hypothesis: Same as r1c1, but with ppo_epochs set to 2. Under the fixed budget this nearly doubles environment samples (about 217k versus 119k).
